Strengthen the link to the Australian long-run growth and productivity aims used in the Units 3 and 4 Study Design, so the card matches how the course frames supply-side policy.
match.reason: The bank card teaches the same supply-side idea at a suitable depth, but its examples and framing are from the UK and Singapore and need localising for an Australian VCE course.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point (e-supplyside) mostly teaches the market-based versus interventionist split with UK examples. The new point is about why supply-side policies matter: more and better resources, lower costs and higher productivity allow growth without inflation alongside demand policies. That is a different focus and would need more than small changes.

draft.title: Why supply-side policies matter
card: Supply-side policies aim to raise the economy's productive capacity. They do this by improving the quantity and quality of resources such as labour and capital, by cutting business costs, and by lifting productivity (output per unit of input).
Demand policies, such as changes to government spending, taxes and interest rates, work on aggregate demand. If demand grows faster than capacity, it can push up prices.
Supply-side policies shift aggregate supply to the right. The economy can then produce more at each price level, so output can grow with less pressure on prices.
Supply-side effects usually take years to appear. So governments use them alongside demand policies, which act more quickly, to pursue sustainable growth and low inflation.
draft.remember: Supply-side policies raise capacity, so growth can come with less pressure on prices.

a.q: Why can supply-side policies help the economy grow without causing inflation?
opts: They raise productive capacity, so more can be produced
They cut aggregate demand, so spending grows more slowly
They lift prices, so firms are paid more for each good
They raise interest rates, so households borrow less
a.why: Supply-side policies shift aggregate supply to the right, so output can rise without demand outrunning capacity. The option about cutting demand describes a demand policy, which works on spending rather than on what the economy can produce.
a.clue: Think about what these policies change: spending or capacity?

b.q: A state government funds new training and cuts business costs, while the central bank keeps interest rates steady. Which result is most likely over several years?
opts: Capacity rises, so output can grow with less price pressure
Aggregate demand falls, so output and prices both drop
Capacity stays fixed, so output can only grow with inflation
Output rises at once, because supply policies act quickly
b.why: Training and lower costs improve resources and productivity, which shifts aggregate supply to the right over time. The last option is tempting but wrong: the card says supply-side effects usually take years, so they do not act at once.
b.clue: Do these policies change spending now, or what the economy can produce later?

a.best: They raise productive capacity, so more can be produced

b.best: Capacity rises, so output can grow with less price pressure

problems.detail: Why (b) calls the 'acts quickly' option 'the last option', but the options are shuffled and the last option shown is the correct answer. Students would read the why as rejecting the right answer. Name the option by its content, not its position.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and the card is accurate. However, why (b) refers to the 'last option' as wrong when, in this order, the last option is the correct answer, so it should name the 'output rises at once' option by its content.
